newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: NZ warns on proposed Australia car tariff freeze.
newsitem.headline: NZ warns on proposed Australia car tariff freeze.

text.p: New Zealand Foreign Affairs and Trade Minister Don McKinnon said on Thursday a proposed freeze on tariff cuts to protect the Australian car industry could put at risk multilateral trade in the Asia Pacific region.

McKinnon, speaking after a routine ministerial meeting with Australian foreign minister Alexander Downer, said the whole point of the APEC forum's tariff reduction programme was greater multilateral trade which was of enormous benefit to the region.
"If one country decides to stop, others get nervous, domestic politics come to play and the whole process becomes then in doubt," he told a news conference after the talks.
"So from time to time, as politicians, we just have to grit our teeth, and hope we can get through such a thing like this," McKinnon said.

South Australia state Premier John Olsen has called for a 10 year freeze on reductions in Australian car industry tariffs, as the federal government considers assistance arrangements to the industry beyond 2000, when tariffs are due to be 15 percent.
South Australia is home to two major car manufacturing plants, owned by Mitsubishi Motors of Japan and the Australian subsidiary of General Motors.
A draft report by the Productivity Commission has proposed further cutting tariffs to five percent by 2004, prompting warnings that car manufacturers could pull out of Australia.

"I am not about to get into a debate on Australian internal politics but certainly the signals (a freeze) would send would not be the kind of signals that would be in the overall interests of Australia or New Zealand or any others," McKinnon said.

"If New Zealand manufacturers said to the New Zealand government 'we would like to see a freeze on tariffs at their present level until we get through a certain period' we are just sending a signal to all our trading partners throughout the world that we are opting out of the APEC process," he said.

Downer would not speculate on future tariff arrangements, saying the government would develop its position following a final Productivity Commission report in May and consultation with the industry and other interested parties.

Australia had seen a very significant reduction in its overall level of protection in the past decade, but there had also been significant, albeit patchy, reductions in south east and north east Asia, he said.
"We will be working very hard to ensure that other countries reduce their protections and we do not do this just on our own," Downer said.
